result.text: A guest enters the restaurant when feeling hungry.
He chooses a dish from the changing meal range and waits until it is his turn.
Following this he places his order with the employee.
The employee enters the order into the POS system and collects the money from the guest.
After the payment, the employee sets up a buzzer and passes it on to the guest with the following information: "When the buzzer rings, your dinner is ready".
Afterwards the employee informs the chef of the new meal order.
The chef prepares the meal and places it in the service hatch.
He then informs the employee that he has placed the finished meal in the service hatch.
As soon as the employee is aware that the meal is ready he sets off the guest's buzzer.
This is how the guest finds out that his meal is ready for collection.
He can pick up his meal and eat it.
As soon as the guest appears at the service hatch, the employee hands over his meal.
Should a guest not react to the buzzer, the employee calls for him after 5 minutes, if necessary several times in a row.

result.text: A guest enters the restaurant when feeling hungry.
He chooses a dish from the changing meal range and waits until it is his turn.
Following this he places his order with the employee.
The employee enters the order into the POS system and collects the money from the guest.

Afterwards the employee informs the chef of the new meal order.
The chef prepares the meal and places it in the service hatch.
He then informs the employee that he has placed the finished meal in the service hatch.
As soon as the employee is aware that the meal is ready he sets off the guest's buzzer.
This is how the guest finds out that his meal is ready for collection.
He can pick up his meal and eat it.
As soon as the guest appears at the service hatch, the employee hands over his meal.
Should a guest not react to the buzzer, the employee calls for him after 5 minutes, if necessary several times in a row.

Should a guest not react to the buzzer, the employee calls for him after 5 minutes, if necessary several times in a row.

Use short, faithful labels in the input language. Prefer verb-object activity names and meaningful business triggers or outcomes for events.
For a message event, put messageRef on its bpmn:messageEventDefinition, never on the event element itself.

Follow the BPMN XML schema: never put a documentation element directly inside bpmn:definitions, and never nest a sequenceFlow inside a task, gateway or event. If you add an ioSpecification, it must contain its dataInput and dataOutput elements first, then at least one inputSet and one outputSet, even if empty: <bpmn:inputSet/><bpmn:outputSet/>.
Use bpmn:callActivity only to invoke a separately defined reusable process or global task; make calledElement resolvable in the intended model context.

result.rule: When the description gives contextual details or examples alongside a single activity, without presenting them as separate actions: label the BPMN task with its core action and object; omit contextual details and qualifiers that are not needed to identify the activity

When the description states a specific business trigger or process outcome for a start or end event: Label the corresponding BPMN event with a concise phrase that preserves that stated trigger or outcome, rather than using a generic label such as “start” or “end”.

When the description states a core activity and separately describes a condition or later outcome that marks its completion: Label the BPMN activity with its core action and object; do not add the separately stated completion condition or later outcome to the activity label.

When the description names an activity or outcome with multiple stated actions, alternatives, or a distinguishing object or participant.: Label the corresponding BPMN activity or event so its described scope remains identifiable. Preserve materially stated actions, alternatives, and objects or participants; do not substitute a broader or different action or add unsupported details.

result.text: A guest enters the restaurant when feeling hungry.
He chooses a dish from the changing meal range and waits until it is his turn.
Following this he places his order with the employee.
The employee enters the order into the POS system and collects the money from the guest.
After the payment, the employee sets up a buzzer and passes it on to the guest with the following information: "When the buzzer rings, your dinner is ready".
Afterwards the employee informs the chef of the new meal order.
The chef prepares the meal and places it in the service hatch.
He then informs the employee that he has placed the finished meal in the service hatch.
As soon as the employee is aware that the meal is ready he sets off the guest's buzzer.
This is how the guest finds out that his meal is ready for collection.
He can pick up his meal and eat it.
As soon as the guest appears at the service hatch, the employee hands over his meal.
Should a guest not react to the buzzer, the employee calls for him after 5 minutes, if necessary several times in a row.

result.process_description:
A guest enters the restaurant when feeling hungry. 
He chooses a dish from the changing meal range and waits until it is his turn. 
Following this he places his order with the employee. The employee enters the order into the POS system and collects the money from the guest. 
After the payment, the employee sets up a buzzer and passes it on to the guest with the following information: 
"When the buzzer rings, your dinner is ready". 
Afterwards the employee informs the chef of the new meal order. 
The chef prepares the meal and places it in the service hatch. 
He then informs the employee that he has placed the finished meal in the service hatch. 
As soon as the employee is aware that the meal is ready he sets off the guest's buzzer. 
This is how the guest finds out that his meal is ready for collection. 
He can pick up his meal and eat it. 
As soon as the guest appears at the service hatch, the employee hands over his meal. 
Should a guest not react to the buzzer, the employee calls for him after 5 minutes, if necessary several times in a row.

result.rule: Sequence flows may cross lanes in one process. Use message flows across participant pools, never between lanes.
Use sequence flows inside one participant process and message flows between different participants. Never use sequence flow across pools.
Do not create separate pools for ordinary internal roles unless the description treats them as independent communicating participants.
Several unconditional outgoing flows from one activity can all proceed. Use a gateway when the description requires a decision or synchronization.
Model every distinct activity, event, participant, decision, branch, loop, message and outcome stated in the description. Do not invent process facts.
Distinguish message tasks from message events: a task models performed work; an event models a message occurrence affecting flow.

args.text: When a process description says one participant informs, signals, calls, or hands something to another participant, model a message flow from the communicating participant's activity to the receiving participant's message-catching event. Do not model an arrival or other ordinary occurrence as a message unless the description says it communicates something.

result.rule: When the description states that one participant requests information or action from another participant and that the other participant provides a response: Model the request and response as a connected interaction: use sequence flows within a participant’s process and message flows between distinct participant pools, rather than an unrelated detached start-to-end chain.

When the description identifies a user-facing software interface as a recipient of information produced by a process and describes that information being communicated to the interface: Model the interface as a separate participant pool and represent the exchange with message flows between that pool and the process; do not model the exchange solely as internal events or activities.

When the description assigns actions to distinct participants and describes information, requests, or responses passing between them: Model each independent participant in a separate pool and represent each described communication with a message flow from sender to receiver, using valid interaction nodes or participant boundaries.

When the description identifies an outside person or organization as the destination of a handoff but describes no subsequent action or response by that recipient: Model the handoff as an activity in the modeled process; do not add a separate participant pool and message flow solely because the recipient is named.
